findings.title: Cross-interview enjoyment of open-ended, discussion-based inquiry (2.a)
findings.description: Students in both I01 and I02 express clear preference for labs structured around open discussion and understanding rather than fixed procedures with predetermined results. I01 students describe enjoying talking 'freely' about results and physics, while I02 students explicitly value that the lab 'handler meget om forståelse' and is 'mere konstruktivt end at have et lab'.

findings.title: Positive affective reactions ('nice', 'fedt', 'sejt') recur strongly in I02, moderately in I01
findings.description: Both interviews contain multiple short affective exclamations expressing enjoyment (e.g. 'nice', 'wow', 'fedt', 'sejt') tied to lab activities, but I02 shows a markedly higher density and intensity of such expressions than I01, suggesting a more uniformly positive experience in I02.

findings.title: Ambivalence about lack of defined/precise procedure (1.b vs 2.a)
findings.description: In I01, students describe expecting more precision and defined placement instructions (1.b), and one student explicitly states the experience was 'not as fun' and less defined than expected, while another frames the openness as 'both positive and negative'. This creates a tension with the otherwise positive framing of open-ended discovery seen elsewhere (2.a), showing the same lack of structure was experienced as both liberating and frustrating within the same interview.

findings.title: Problem-solving experiences (1.c) diverge in nature between interviews: conceptual vs. procedural/technical
findings.description: In I01, problem-solving quotes center on conceptual/interpretive struggles (understanding polarization, needing theoretical background, pre-lab explanation being too fast). In I02, problem-solving quotes center on procedural/technical troubleshooting (small-degree adjustments to find interference, table stabilization, touching mirrors causing wobble, imperfect lenses). This suggests the same code captures qualitatively different kinds of difficulty depending on the lab context.

findings.title: Relevance of quantum topic to students' field disputed within I01
findings.description: One student in I01 explicitly states the quantum content is 'not really our area' since most of the group does astrophysics, directly questioning the lab's relevance (3.d), while other students in the same interview (2.a, 3.a, 3.b) express enjoyment, conceptual gains, and engagement with the very same lab content, creating a contradiction between perceived relevance and expressed value/enjoyment.

findings.title: Experimentalist, hands-on identity/engagement (2.c) appears only in I02 but is consistent and repeated
findings.description: Multiple I02 quotes from different students converge on describing the lab as allowing direct, intuitive, hands-on reasoning ('du sidder og drejer', 'visuelt resonere', 'fri til at lege med det'), forming a consistent pattern of experimentalist engagement absent from I01 (where 2.c has zero counts), suggesting this lab format specifically fostered a hands-on identity for I02 students.

findings.title: Playful/childlike discovery metaphor as a recurring but uncoded motif
findings.description: Student 1 in I02 uses a vivid metaphor comparing hands-on experimentation to a child discovering the properties of mixing potato starch and water, an intuitive discovery framing that recurs across two quotes discussing the same experience but is not captured by any single codebook code specifically about metaphorical/playful sense-making.

findings.title: Forward-looking usefulness framed as career/specialization guidance (3.c) only in I02
findings.description: I02 students link the lab experience to future academic/career considerations, such as informatics applications and choosing a specialization, a forward-looking usefulness framing that does not appear at all in I01 (0 counts for 3.c), suggesting a distinct thematic emphasis in I02 not mirrored in I01.

findings.title: Peer collaboration and reliance on classmates' prior knowledge (social relations)
findings.description: Students in I01 reference relying on peers with prior optics knowledge to make sense of the lab ('some of my friends had optics so I was playing around', 'if we didn't have that we would have no idea'), highlighting peer dynamics and knowledge-sharing that are not captured by any codebook code but recur as a social-collaboration theme.
